16.0.s.en: (1) The reign of Ahaz over Judah

16.0.0.en: In the seventeenth year of Pekah the son of Remaliah king of Israel, Jehoahaz became king over Judah, after the death of Jotham his father. Because of his evil, the writer of the book removed the name of Jehovah, that is, God, from his name and called him Ahaz, because he worshiped idols. He began to reign at the age of twenty and reigned sixteen years, and we are told (ch. 18:2) that his son Hezekiah began to reign at the age of twenty-five. Of course Ahaz could not have begotten his son Hezekiah at the age of ten, because Ahaz died at the age of thirty-six, so that Ahaz would have been eleven years old when Hezekiah was born, that is, he would have begotten him at the age of ten. The truth is that Hezekiah reigned alone at the age of twenty-five, but he had reigned a period before that with his father, and his age then, when he began to reign, was less than twenty-five, perhaps twenty or fifteen; we do not know exactly, because the Holy Bible did not mention this. It was a custom among the kings to make their young sons kings with them, to secure the kingdom and to train them in managing the kingdom. And he did not do what was right like David his forefather the king, but walked in evil and the worship of idols.

16.1.0.en: Sadly, Ahaz imitated the kings of Israel, all of whom worshiped idols, and did not imitate his righteous father and forefather. So he served the god of the children of Ammon and offered his sons as burnt offerings to them, and not merely one son, as is mentioned here; for the Book of Chronicles mentions that he offered more than one son (2 Chr 28:3). And he worshiped the gods of the original inhabitants of the land, the pagans whom God drove out by the hand of Joshua, and offered sacrifices to the pagan gods on the high places and the hills and under the green trees which they had set apart for the worship of the pagan gods; that is, he went to extremes in the worship of the many pagan gods. His mention of every green tree shows how widespread the worship of idols was in the age of Ahaz; for he led his people astray and led them in the worship of idols.

16.1.1.en: And perhaps the reason for Ahaz’s going to extremes in the worship of idols was his fear of the alliance of Rezin king of Aram and Pekah the son of Remaliah king of Israel and their readiness to fight him; so instead of taking refuge in God, he took refuge in the pagan gods in great number, although Isaiah the prophet had reassured him that if he believed in God no harm would come to him (Isa 7:4-16), and that these two kings would die and their lands be forsaken, but he did not believe and lived in fear and the worship of idols. Likewise the prophet Micah rebuked him (Mic 6:6-8), because he offered his sons as burnt offerings to the god Molech, but he did not repent.

16.1.2.en: Do not reject the warnings and admonitions of God to you, whether in the Holy Bible, or from your father of confession and all those around you, lest you be exposed to error and destruction and live in fear and turmoil. Believe in the power of God which is with you, and you will live in tranquility.

16.2.0.en: Rezin king of Aram and Pekah the son of Remaliah king of Israel feared Assyria, and so they united together to be a power that Assyria could not overcome, and they tried to unite with Ahaz king of Judah, but he refused, because of his inclination to rely on Assyria. So Rezin and Pekah rose against him to fight him and were able to be victorious over him in part, killing some of his soldiers (2 Chr 28:5-8), and they besieged Jerusalem, but they were not able to overcome him completely, and so they withdrew.

16.3.0.en: During the invasions of Rezin king of Aram into the kingdom of Judah, he was able to take Elath, which is an important port on the Gulf of Aqaba at its northern end, the present Eilat, and he drove the Jews out of it and settled the Arameans in it.

16.4.0.en: Ahaz was angered and afraid of the invasions of Aram and Israel, and instead of relying on God, he sent to the king of Assyria to ask his help, to protect him from the two kings of Aram and Israel.

16.4.1.en: This agreed with the ambitions of Assyria to take all the surrounding countries, and Ahaz’s request encouraged him to take the kingdom of Israel and Aram, and in this the captivity of the kingdom of Israel was accomplished; for the evils of Ahaz were a cause of the captivity of the northern kingdom. The weakness of Ahaz appears in his saying to the king of Assyria, “I am thy servant and thy son,” for he declares his complete submission to him. History does not mention that Ahaz was among the list of those who paid tribute to the king of Assyria, and this means that he was completely enslaved to him.

16.5.0.en: As a declaration of his submission to the king of Assyria, Ahaz took the silver and gold that were in the house of the Lord and sent them as a present to the king of Assyria, that he might be pleased with him and protect him. This clearly confirms Ahaz’s reliance on the powers of the world and his lack of faith in God, so that he plundered the house of the Lord to please the pagan king of Assyria, and in this he halted the service in the house of the Lord; so he encourages and spreads the worship of idols and closes the house of the Lord and stops its worship.

16.6.0.en: Kir: a city lying between the two rivers, and it is the original homeland of the Arameans.

16.6.1.en: The king of Assyria seized the opportunity to fulfill his ambitions, and so he answered the call of Ahaz, not out of love for him, but to fulfill his aims of taking the world around him, and he killed Rezin and took Damascus, the capital of the Arameans.

16.6.2.en: God wants to support you, so why do you look for other means and so expose yourself to troubles? Know that the world works for its own interest and not for your interest, and that God alone is the One who loves you and wants your salvation, so do not draw away from Him, however dangers surround you.

16.7.0.en: Ahaz went to Damascus to congratulate the king of Assyria on his victories over the Arameans and to declare his submission to him, and he saw how the king of Assyria had taken control of the city and set up in it a great altar to the gods of the Assyrians, in order to break the identity, nationality and religion of the Arameans, so that they would worship the gods of the Assyrians. And because Ahaz did not care about the worship of God and worshiped idols, he flattered the king of Assyria by taking the form and dimensions of the Assyrian altar and sending them to Urijah the high priest, to make an altar like it inside the house of the Lord, although it was God who had given David in writing the details of building the Temple, and David handed them to Solomon, who carried them out exactly in obedience to the word of God (1 Chr 28:19); but Ahaz here despises God and His Temple to please the king of Assyria.

16.8.0.en: Urijah the priest carried out all that Ahaz asked and built an altar according to the designs sent to him by King Ahaz. And he completed its building before the return of the king from Damascus. This shows the weakness of Urijah the high priest and his laxity in the right of God and His house to please the king. It also shows the weakness of the worship of God and of the priestly leadership in the days of Ahaz, and the going astray of the people after foreign gods. And we marvel before the faith of Naaman the Syrian, who took earth from the land of Israel to set up an altar to the Lord in Damascus, while Ahaz the Jew, who did not believe in God, sets up in the house of the Lord an altar after the pattern of the pagan altars.

16.9.0.en: When Ahaz returned from Damascus he saw the great altar that he had charged Urijah the priest to build, and he admired it. And in pride that reaches beyond the priesthood, he came forward himself to offer a peace offering and himself sprinkled its blood on this altar, after he had offered his offering on this altar and poured out on it his drink offering of wine. Here he erred in two things:

16.9.1.en: 1- His usurping the priesthood in offering the sacrifice.

16.9.2.en: 2- Making an altar contrary to the commandments of God, which he set up after the pattern of the altars of the pagans, and he even set it up in place of the bronze altar of God and removed the other and put it aside, as we shall see in (v. 14).

16.10.0.en: Ahaz set up the new great altar before the house of the Lord, which is on the east side; before it stood the bronze altar, then the Sea in which the priests washed, then the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies. So that the new altar might be the main altar and the sacrifices of the children of Israel be offered on it, Ahaz commanded that the bronze altar be removed and moved aside to the north side, that is, on the right of one entering the house of the Lord. This is a clear ritual violation, meaning Ahaz’s concern to please the king of Assyria instead of pleasing the Lord.

16.11.0.en: King Ahaz commanded Urijah the priest to offer the morning burnt offering and the evening offering, and the king’s burnt offering and his offering, with the burnt offering of the people and their offering and the drink offerings of their wine, on the altar which he called the great altar. And it was set apart for sprinkling the blood of every burnt offering or sacrifice. As for the bronze altar, it would be for the king, when he wished to inquire of the Lord in some matter. This means Ahaz’s attempt to get rid of the bronze altar, by putting it aside and saying, if I want to ask God about something I will use this altar; in truth he wants to get rid of this altar, but after a while, so as not to stir up the priests and the people. And Urijah the priest did all that King Ahaz asked.

16.12.0.en: After Ahaz had taken the gold and silver that were in the house of the Lord and worship in it was neglected and he had replaced the bronze altar with his great altar, he felt that the bronze Sea, in which the priests washed before entering the Holy Place, was unimportant, and likewise the ten lavers that Solomon had made for washing the sacrifices in them; for he in general was not concerned with worship in the house of the Lord but with all the worship of idols in the city of Jerusalem. Therefore he took the bronze bases on which the lavers rested and put the lavers on the ground. He also took the twelve bronze oxen on which the Sea rested; perhaps he wanted to make use of their bronze. And he put the Sea on a row of stones. In sum, Ahaz despised the house of the Lord and thought of his own interest and of acquiring bronze to benefit him in the costs of his kingdom.

16.13.0.en: There was in the house of the Lord a large hall in which the people gathered on the Sabbath day for worship, and since Ahaz neglected the sanctification of the Sabbath day and the worship of God in His Temple, he removed this hall, that is, the covert. There was also a special entrance for the king from his house to the Temple of God, and he removed it too, because he did not want the worship of God in His Temple; all this was to please the king of Assyria, and in this Ahaz declares to him that he has neglected the worship of God and worships the gods of the Assyrians, for whom he had set up altars in all parts of Jerusalem.

16.13.1.en: If a person gives himself up to sin, he slips into its depths and does evils without limit, as Ahaz did. But you, O man of God, hold fast to the worship of God in His Church and beware of sin. And if you fall, repent quickly and return to God, and He will cleanse you from every evil, for He loves the weak and supports them but is greatly angered at the rebellious and those who take liberties.

16.14.s.en: (4) The death of Ahaz and the reign of Hezekiah

16.14.0.en: The rest of what Ahaz did during the period of his rule is written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah. Ahaz died and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and his son Hezekiah reigned after him. The evils of Ahaz were very many and were written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah, which, as we mentioned, is not the Book of Chronicles found in the Holy Bible. We notice that because of the multitude of the evils of Ahaz he was not buried in the tombs of the kings of Judah, but was buried in ordinary graves in the city of David (2 Chr 28:27). And God allowed this king to die young, for he died at the age of thirty-six, so that Judah might be rid of his many evils.

16.14.1.en: In the age of the wicked Ahaz lived the great prophet Isaiah, to proclaim the voice of God. So be assured that God does not leave Himself without a witness, and do not be troubled by the multitude of evils around you. Be faithful in obeying the commandments of God and know that there are many who still worship God as you do, so complete your striving that you may receive the Kingdom. The captivity of Israel and the sins of the people of God

17.0.s.en: (1) Hoshea and the captivity of Israel

17.0.0.en: Hoshea the son of Elah reigned over Israel in Samaria, after he assassinated Pekah the son of Remaliah, and the period of his rule lasted nine years, and that was in the twelfth year of King Ahaz, king of the children of Judah.

17.1.0.en: He committed evils, but his conduct was less perverse than that of the kings of Israel who preceded him.

17.2.0.en: Shalmaneser king of Assyria threatened him with invasion, and so Hoshea submitted to him and paid him tribute, that he might confirm him over the kingdom of Israel, and in this he became his vassal. That is because Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria was the one who made Hoshea king over Israel, as the history of Assyria mentions. Hoshea remained submissive to Assyria until the death of Tiglath-pileser, and after that he rebelled against Assyria, and Shalmaneser, the new king of Assyria, attacked him and subjected Hoshea to himself, and he paid tribute to Assyria.

17.3.0.en: Hoshea remained far from God and relied on his own thinking in his rebellion against Assyria and then his submission to it, and so he thought of rebelling again against Shalmaneser and not paying him tribute, seizing the opportunity of Shalmaneser’s being occupied with fighting Phoenicia, that is, present-day Lebanon, and he sent to ally himself with the king of Egypt, who is called So. The king of Assyria discovered this alliance and the treachery of Hoshea, because he had not paid the tribute, so Shalmaneser sent and seized Hoshea and put him in prison, and the kingdom of Israel was left without a leader, which made it easier afterward, when Samaria was besieged, for it to fall into the hand of the Assyrians.

17.3.1.en: The prophet Hosea had warned King Hoshea against allying with So king of Egypt (Hos 7:11, 12:1), but he did not obey God, for he relied on human power, and the result was his humiliation in prison. The nine years of his reign are counted until the fall of Samaria and not until his being put in prison, that is, King Hoshea was put in prison in the sixth year of his reign.

17.4.0.en: The king of Assyria attacked all the lands of Israel and went to Samaria, the capital, and besieged it for three years. And Shalmaneser died during the siege of Samaria and Sargon succeeded him, into whose hand Samaria fell. The kingdom of Israel was taken captive in three stages, which took sixty-five years, and they are:

17.4.1.en: 1- The first attack at the hand of Tiglath-pileser, a year after the prophecy of Isaiah.

17.4.2.en: 2- The second attack at the hand of Shalmaneser, twenty years after the prophecy of Isaiah.

17.4.3.en: 3- The third and last attack at the hand of Esarhaddon, after a period of sixty-five years from the prophecy of Isaiah, and this was the complete captivity of Israel. During that time Manasseh king of Judah was seized and imprisoned in Babylon for a period, and then he pardoned him and returned him to Jerusalem. The Assyrian writings mention that Shalmaneser took captive 27,290 of Israel and took fifty war chariots.

17.5.0.en: Halah: the name of a province in the empire of Assyria, in Mesopotamia, near the town of Gozan. Habor, the river of Gozan: a river in Mesopotamia, the river Khabur, which flows south through Mesopotamia and after 300 km meets the eastern branch of the Euphrates. Media: a land lying east of Assyria, now part of present-day Iran.

17.5.1.en: In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria and carried the children of Israel captive and sent them to the countries subject to the kingdom of Assyria and settled them in several cities: Halah, and Habor by the river of Gozan, and the cities of the Medes.

17.5.2.en: The Holy Bible does not mention when Hoshea died, because he was a wicked king; God did not care to record his death and burial, and of course no king succeeded him over Israel, because it had come to an end as a kingdom and had become a province subject to the kingdom of Assyria.

17.5.3.en: When you feel your weakness before the powers of the world, take refuge in God and do not look for human solutions; they alone will not benefit you if God does not bless them, for He is the source of your protection and your strength and the salvation of your soul.

17.6.s.en: (2) The sins of the children of Israel before the captivity

17.6.0.en: It may seem at first sight that the captivity of Israel took place because of the power of Assyria, which swept over the world around it and took many countries, among them the kingdom of Israel. But the true cause of the captivity of Israel is its sins. These verses mention a list of the sins of Israel and also of the kingdom of Judah, which fell some time after it, also because of its sins. And the first sin it mentions is that after God had freed them from the slavery of Egypt and its idols, they returned and worshiped the foreign gods, in addition to their worship of God.

17.7.0.en: And since the children of Israel mixed with the nations and worshiped their gods and also took from them their pagan customs and their evil forms of worship, they added to these evils their following and encouraging of their wicked kings, beginning with Jeroboam, who split the kingdom of Israel, that is, the ten tribes, and set up the idols in Bethel and Dan, and then all the kings of Israel followed him, down to Hoshea, the last of their kings, for all of them worshiped idols and some of them went to extremes in these pagan forms of worship, such as Ahab.

17.8.0.en: The tower of the watchmen: a small farm with a watchtower.

17.8.1.en: The worship of idols began among the children of Israel secretly in their houses, or in hiding, and then it spread, and the children of Israel went to extremes in their evil, and offered worship to the foreign gods on the high places. And these strange forms of worship spread throughout all the land of the children of Israel, from the very smallest village to the large fortified city.

17.8.2.en: Be on your guard against sin when it creeps in on you, for it enters your thought first, and then it comes by way of sight or thought, and presses on you and changes your speech, and then defiles your deeds and enslaves you. So drive sin out from its beginning by repentance and by keeping away from the sources of evil, however dear they are in your sight.

17.9.0.en: They made idols and poles on the hills and under every large tree with wide shade; that is, pagan worship continued to spread until it was in every place.

17.10.0.en: The people of God offered complete acts of worship to the idols by offering sacrifices and burning incense, and indeed they did, like the nations whom God drove out before them, vile evils to please the idols, such as fornication and every uncleanness. In this they defied God by their disobedience and provoked Him; for God had commanded them clearly in the Law of Moses to keep away from the worship of idols (Ex 20:1-5).

17.11.0.en: The seer: one who sees visions, by which God makes known to him His commands, to deliver them to the people.

17.11.1.en: The Lord sent to Israel and Judah many prophets and seers, calling them to leave their evil practices and to walk according to the commandments of the Lord, His statutes and the judgments of His Law.

17.12.0.en: They hardened their necks: that is, they turned their backs to God and were stubborn against Him. The expression is taken from an animal, such as a horse, that stiffens its neck so that the rider cannot lead it.

17.12.1.en: They did not heed the calls and warnings of the prophets, but continued in their error and went to extremes in their stubbornness, like their fathers, who refused to believe in the Lord their God.

17.13.0.en: His statutes: His acts of worship.

17.13.1.en: His covenant: that He would be their God and they would be His people.

17.13.2.en: His testimonies: His commandments and His Law.

17.13.3.en: The children of Israel refused to submit to their covenant with God, to be a special people who worship Him alone. And they left His worship and His commandments, which they transgressed, and these bore witness to their perversion. And they followed the nations in the worship of the foreign, vain gods, which profit nothing, and so they became a perverted people, of no value, like the rest of the nations, and they lost the blessing of God and His protection of them. And because the worship of idols is vain, whoever worships idols becomes vain himself, that is, without value.

17.14.0.en: The two calves: that is, the two idols that Jeroboam the son of Nebat set up in the kingdom of Israel, in Bethel and Dan.

17.14.1.en: Groves: the plural of grove, which is a tall pole set up on the high places for the worship of the moon, with altars built beside this pole.

17.14.2.en: The host of heaven: the heavenly bodies and stars which the Assyrians worship.

17.14.3.en: Baal: one of the most famous pagan gods in the land of Canaan, and the sun was a symbol of him.

17.14.4.en: Israel neglected the commandments of God and His worship in His Temple in Jerusalem and worshiped the golden calves in Bethel and Dan, in addition to the gods of the nations, and so they set up poles and temples for them.

17.15.0.en: The people of God plunged into the worship of idols, and so they burned their sons in the fire to please Molech the god of the children of Ammon, and they sought the unseen through diviners and sorcerers, who deal with demons, and they felt that good or evil would come upon them from strange things, such as the falling of a morsel from the mouth or the passing of a gazelle across the road; that is, they took omens of good and of evil, and in this they sold themselves to evil, that is, became slaves of the pagan gods, and provoked God.

17.15.1.en: All these demonic practices still influence some societies around us, so let us avoid them completely, for the Scripture warns us against them in the strongest warning (Deut 18:10-12).

17.16.0.en: Because of all these evils God was angry with His people in the kingdom of Israel and allowed Assyria to take them captive, and only the kingdom of Judah remained, because it still worshiped God in His Temple in Jerusalem, even if it sometimes fell into the worship of idols, and so God gave it another opportunity to repent. But it did not repent, and He allowed its captivity a hundred and thirty-five years later at the hand of Babylon. And the word of God about the kingdom of Israel, that He removed them out of His sight, is the hardest thing, that is, the protection and blessing of God left them and He refused to dwell among them, and so He scattered them among the nations to humble them, that perhaps they might repent.

17.17.0.en: After God gave the kingdom of Judah an opportunity to repent, sadly it did as the kingdom of Israel did and worshiped idols, and did not learn from the captivity of Israel and did not fear God, and so it halted between the worship of God and the worship of idols.

17.18.0.en: The Lord rejected all the children of Israel and punished them, delivering them into the hand of spoilers and casting them out of His sight.

17.19.0.en: Jeroboam the son of Nebat split off with the ten tribes and set up a kingdom which he called Israel, and the kingdom of Judah remained under the rule of the descendants of David. With the separation of the kingdom of Israel it walked in the worship of idols and began to draw away from God, until its captivity to Assyria was accomplished.

17.20.0.en: By the children of Israel is meant the people of God in the kingdom of Israel, who worshiped the golden calves that Jeroboam set up; that is, the people continued in the worship of idols until God allowed their captivity, that is, He turned His face away from them and abandoned them, as He had warned them many times by the mouth of His prophets, before this Assyrian captivity was accomplished. But in the end, because of their insistence on provoking God, He was compelled to leave them to captivity and humiliation, that perhaps they might repent.

17.21.s.en: (3) The worship of God and of idols after the captivity

17.21.0.en: Babylon: a city on both banks of the river Euphrates; its region was anciently known as the land of Shinar. Cuth: a city belonging to Babylon, lying twenty-four kilometers northeast of Babylon. Ava: a Babylonian city.

17.21.1.en: Hamath: a city on the Orontes river north of Hermon, about one hundred and ninety kilometers north of Damascus.

17.21.2.en: Sepharvaim: a town lying on both banks of the river Euphrates, twenty-six kilometers southwest of Baghdad.

17.21.3.en: The king of Assyria removed the children of Israel from the cities of Samaria and settled them in the cities that Assyria controlled, and brought people from Assyrian cities: Babylon, Cuth, Ava, Hamath and Sepharvaim. And he settled them in the cities of Samaria instead of the children of Israel, and they dwelt in its cities.

17.21.4.en: That was the policy of some empires in earlier times, which aimed at mixing the peoples with one another, in order to guard against the feeling of nationhood and attachment to the land; that is, the kings of Assyria, in their three invasions of the kingdom of Israel, did this, and so did their successors among the kings of Assyria.

17.22.0.en: After a large number of the Jews were deported to the land of Assyria and a number of the inhabitants of the land of Assyria were settled in their place, the number of inhabitants became fewer and the land was wide for them, so the number of lions in the land increased, and this was by the permission of God, and they devoured some of them and they were very afraid. This was a divine chastening of the pagans, that they might understand that this land has a God whom they ought to obey, for they are pagans who believe in a plurality of gods. And we notice that they were able to understand that there is a mighty God of this land, and they feared Him. But on the other hand the Jews, who knew that God is the owner of all lands, did not fear Him and neglected His commandments and worshiped the foreign gods, and so God drove them out of His land.

17.22.1.en: If only you would learn from all those around you, for you may find in some who are far from God virtues that you need to learn, and even to go deeper in them, because you have an opportunity, by the power of God, to master them. And according to the measure of your humility and your love of being a disciple, God will give to you.

17.23.0.en: They sent to the king of Assyria, saying that the people whom he had brought to the cities of Samaria to settle there did not know the ordinances of the god of this land, and so he sent lions among them which devoured them. There was a belief among the ancient pagan peoples that every land has its god, whom it must worship.

17.24.0.en: The king of Assyria commanded that one of the priests whom they had carried away captive from that land be sent there, to return to Samaria and dwell there and teach the new settlers the ordinances of the god of the land. This priest was not one of the priests of God of the descendants of Aaron, but one of the priests of the calves that Jeroboam the son of Nebat set up; he was Jewish in origin and knew God and the books of Moses, but did not have the rank of the priesthood, so his information about God was confused, but he knew about God better than the nations, who did not know Him at all.

17.25.0.en: One of the captive priests who had been taken from Samaria did indeed come and returned there and dwelt in Bethel and taught them how they should fear the Lord and what His ordinances were. And Bethel is where one of the calves that Jeroboam the son of Nebat set up was found. This priest may have been from Bethel, and so he taught them the Law of Moses but also taught them the worship of the golden calf.

17.26.0.en: Each of those foreign nations made the idols of its gods and put them in the temples which the Samaritans had built on the hills, each nation in the cities in which it was settled. And so they worshiped God and held to the Law of Moses, but at the same time worshiped their idols; that is, they considered God a god among the gods, respected Him and feared Him and also cared for the rest of the gods, who are demons.

17.26.1.en: And we notice here that this is the first mention of the title Samaritans, that is, the inhabitants of Samaria and its surroundings, who were the dwellers in all of the kingdom of Israel, and the Jews who lived in Jerusalem and Judea shunned them and despised them, because in their worship they associated the pagan gods with God.

17.26.2.en: The Samaritans were of three kinds:

17.26.3.en: 1- Samaritans of Jewish origin who were content with the worship of God and of the two calves that Jeroboam the son of Nebat set up; these were few in number.

17.26.4.en: 2- Samaritans of Jewish origin who worshiped the two calves and added to them other pagan gods whom they worshiped.

17.26.5.en: 3- Samaritans of Gentile origin who worshiped their foreign gods and added to them the worship of God; these were many in number.

17.26.6.en: We also see that the new inhabitants in the cities of Samaria found old houses built on the high places, which the Jews, the inhabitants of the kingdom of Israel, had built in violation of the Law of God, and so they offered to God on the high places and also to the pagan gods.

17.27.0.en: Succoth-benoth: a pagan god, the name meaning the tabernacles of the daughters, that is, the tents of the girls consecrated to fornication in the pagan temples, and it is symbolized by a hen with her chicks.

17.27.1.en: Nergal: the god of war and plague among the Babylonians; his statue is in the form of a lion with two wings and the face of a man. Ashima: he is the god of fire.

17.27.2.en: Nibhaz: a pagan god whose statue is half dog and half man.

17.27.3.en: Adrammelech: the god of the sun, symbolized by the mule.

17.27.4.en: Anammelech: the god of the moon, symbolized by the horse.

17.27.5.en: The new inhabitants in the cities of Samaria worshiped their pagan gods mentioned here and added to them the worship of God.

17.28.0.en: Thus they worshiped the Lord, but at the same time they set up from among themselves priests to serve in the temples of the hills, and they offered their burnt offerings in them. Their worship of God was outward, out of fear of the lions, and was mixed with pagan forms of worship; it was not real godliness toward God but superficial worship, for they did not know God. And this is what Christ said in His conversation with the Samaritan woman, that they worship what they do not know (Jn 4:22).

17.29.0.en: The nations that came to the cities of Samaria outwardly worshiped God, but in truth they did not fear Him nor follow the statutes and ordinances, that is, the acts of worship and the commandments which the Jews perform, in addition to their mixing the superficial worship of God with the worship of idols, whereas God commanded in His commandments that He alone be worshiped.

17.30.0.en: The Lord had made a covenant in former days with the children of Israel and commanded them not to worship other gods, not to bow down to them nor fear them nor offer sacrifices to them, but to fear the Lord alone, who brought them out of Egypt with great power and might; to Him alone they bow down and to Him alone they offer their burnt offerings. This is what the nations ought to have done when they wished to worship God, to become Jews and hold to all His commandments, but they did not do so, and their worship was superficial worship.

17.31.0.en: So those who believe in God must obey the statutes, the ordinances, the Law and the commandments that He gave them, to apply them all the days of their life and not to worship other gods.

17.32.0.en: And they must always remember the covenant He made with them and not worship other gods, but must fear the Lord their God alone, and He will save them and protect them from all their enemies.

17.33.0.en: But those foreign nations refused to listen and continued to practice their old rites, worshiping the Lord outwardly on the one hand and worshiping their idols on the other, and their sons followed this evil conduct, until the time of the writing of this book.

17.33.1.en: The fear of the Lord cannot be united with the paganism of the world. The fear of the Lord means obeying Him, and obedience to the Lord does not tolerate a mixing of complete submission to His will with the love of the world.
